Fairness Metrics based on the AUC in Clinical Predictive AI

CCS: Computing methodologies Artificial intelligenceCCS: Applied computing Health informatics
João Matos email: joao.matos@ndorms.ox.ac.uk Affiliation: Centre for Statistics in Medicine, University of Oxford, Oxford, UK , Ben Van Calster Affiliation: Department of Development and Regeneration, KU Leuven, Leuven, Belgium , Richard D. Riley Affiliation: Department of Applied Health Sciences, University of Birmingham, Birmingham, UK Affiliation: National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Biomedical Research Centre: Birmingham, University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust and University of Birmingham, Birmingham, UK , Paula Dhiman Affiliation: Centre for Statistics in Medicine, University of Oxford, Oxford, UK and Gary S. Collins Affiliation: Department of Applied Health Sciences, University of Birmingham, Birmingham, UK Affiliation: National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Biomedical Research Centre: Birmingham, University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust and University of Birmingham, Birmingham, UK
2026
Abstract.

Fairness evaluation of clinical prediction models for binary outcomes often involves fairness metrics that compare the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC, or c-statistic) across subgroups. However, the AUC has been shown to be a non-collapsible metric, meaning that its subgroup specific and overall values are not directly comparable as often implicitly assumed. This raises important questions about how existing AUC-based fairness metrics should be used and interpreted. We examine eight AUC-based fairness metrics proposed in the literature, including: within-group AUC parity; cross-group AUC (xAUC) parity; gap-to-overall AUC; equity-scaled AUC; minimum-based metrics; xAUC1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}; xAUC0\mathrm{xAUC}^{0}; and xAUC1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1} or xAUC0\mathrm{xAUC}^{0} parity. We characterise their estimands, relate them to the decomposition of overall AUC (into within- and cross-group components), and critically appraise them. We then illustrate their behaviour using simulations based on the EuroSCORE II, a clinical prediction model for in-hospital mortality. Based on our formal analysis, simulations, and clinical examples, we recommend reporting an AUC matrix, containing the overall AUC and all within- and cross-group AUC components, alongside population characteristics. When fairness metrics are needed, we recommend reporting the within-group AUC parity, with cross-group AUC parity providing supplementary information but requiring caution due to its potential conflict with calibration. Metrics involving xAUC1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1} and xAUC0\mathrm{xAUC}^{0} have merit, summarising within- and cross-group AUCs into single values, but their interpretation is non-trivial, and they should be used with caution. Gap-to-overall AUC, equity-scaled AUC, and minimum-based metrics compare quantities that should not be compared and it is unclear how to operationalise them, making them not fit for purpose and generally not recommended.

Keywords: 
AUC, Clinical Prediction Models, Collapsibility, Fairness Metrics

1. Introduction

Clinical prediction models using artificial intelligence (AI) promise to improve patient outcomes and reduce health care costs by informing clinical decision making and risk communication (Topol, 2019). When developing or evaluating a clinical prediction model, assessing its performance is essential to determine its potential value in clinical practice (Van Calster et al., 2025; Collins et al., 2024a; Matos et al., 2024).

Evaluating model performance at the target population level can conceal important differences in model behaviour across subgroups, raising fairness concerns (Oakden-Rayner et al., 2020). It is therefore common to report model performance within relevant subgroups defined by sensitive attributes such as sex or ethnicity. Although variation in model performance across subgroups is expected, understanding the nature and magnitude of differences is central to fairness evaluation (McCradden et al., 2020).

A fairness metric quantifies the extent to which a model’s output does or does not discriminate, according to a particular notion of fairness, against individuals or subgroups defined by a sensitive attribute (Matos et al., 2026c). Most fairness metrics are a comparison of model performance across subgroups, for example through differences, ratios, or other summary functions of subgroup specific performance (Gallifant et al., 2024). Their interpretation therefore depends on the mathematical properties of the underlying performance metric. One mathematical property that is particularly relevant when comparing performance across subgroups is collapsibility (Matos et al., 2026a). A performance metric MM is collapsible if its overall value can be expressed as the weighted average of its subgroup (gg) specific values. If a metric is collapsible, the overall value MoverallM_{\mathrm{overall}} is directly related to the subgroup specific values MgM_{g}; when a metric is non-collapsible, such relationship breaks down, making subgroup and overall values difficult to interpret jointly and potentially misleading fairness assessments.

One important aspect of prediction model performance for which collapsibility is particularly relevant is discrimination, which quantifies the extent to which a model assigns higher estimated probabilities to individuals who experience the event than to those who do not (Van Calster et al., 2025; Pencina and D’Agostino, 2015; Janssens and Martens, 2020). The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC, also known as the c-statistic) is the most widely reported measure of discrimination for clinical prediction models for binary outcomes (Van Calster et al., 2025; Collins et al., 2024b). The AUC has been shown to be non-collapsible (Matos et al., 2026a). Even though numerous fairness metrics that are derived directly from subgroup specific and overall AUC values have been proposed, the implications of AUC non-collapsibility for the interpretation of AUC-based fairness metrics have not been systematically examined.

In this paper, we examine AUC-based fairness metrics for clinical prediction models with binary outcomes. We review eight AUC-based fairness metrics, clarify their target estimands, relate them to the decomposition of the AUC into within- and cross-group components, and illustrate their behaviour using simulations based on the European System for Cardiac Operative Risk Evaluation (EuroSCORE) II (Nashef et al., 2012). Our aim is to clarify when these metrics are informative and how they should be interpreted when evaluating fairness in clinical predictive AI.

2. Non-collapsibility of the AUC

The AUC is a non-collapsible metric (Matos et al., 2026a). The overall AUC cannot, in general, be expressed as a weighted average of subgroup specific AUCs because the AUC considers all event and non-event pairs, including those from different subgroups. Consider a population partitioned into KK mutually exclusive subgroups. Following the notation of Kallus and Zhou (Kallus and Zhou, 2019), let AUCi,j\mathrm{AUC}_{i,j} denote the probability that an individual with the event from subgroup ii is assigned, by the prediction model, a higher estimated probability than an individual without the event from subgroup jj. When i=ji=j, AUCi,i\mathrm{AUC}_{i,i} corresponds to the usual within-group AUC, whereas for i≠ji\neq j, AUCi,j\mathrm{AUC}_{i,j} is the cross-group AUC (xAUC). The overall AUC can therefore be decomposed (Matos et al., 2026a) as:

(1) AUCoverall\displaystyle\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{overall}} =∑i,j=1Kp1ip1​p0jp0​AUCi,j,\displaystyle=\sum_{i,j=1}^{K}\frac{p_{1}^{i}}{p_{1}}\frac{p_{0}^{j}}{p_{0}}\,\mathrm{AUC}_{i,j},

where p1ip_{1}^{i} and p0ip_{0}^{i} denote the numbers (or proportions) of event and non-event observations in subgroup ii, respectively, and p1=∑ip1ip_{1}=\sum_{i}p_{1}^{i} and p0=∑ip0ip_{0}=\sum_{i}p_{0}^{i} denote the corresponding totals. For two subgroups, AA and BB, Equation (1) reduces to

(2) AUCoverall\displaystyle\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{overall}} =p1A​p0Ap1​p0​AUCA+p1A​p0Bp1​p0​xAUCA,B+p1B​p0Ap1​p0​xAUCB,A+p1B​p0Bp1​p0​AUCB\displaystyle=\frac{p_{1}^{A}p_{0}^{A}}{p_{1}p_{0}}\,\mathrm{AUC}_{A}+\frac{p_{1}^{A}p_{0}^{B}}{p_{1}p_{0}}\,\mathrm{xAUC}_{A,B}+\frac{p_{1}^{B}p_{0}^{A}}{p_{1}p_{0}}\,\mathrm{xAUC}_{B,A}+\frac{p_{1}^{B}p_{0}^{B}}{p_{1}p_{0}}\,\mathrm{AUC}_{B}

Equation (1) shows that the overall AUC is a weighted combination of within- and cross-group AUCs. Consequently, the overall AUC is generally not determined by the within-group AUCs alone, hence why it is non-collapsible (Matos et al., 2026a).

3. Review of AUC-based fairness metrics

We now briefly examine eight AUC-based fairness metrics that have been proposed in the literature and summarised by (Matos et al., 2026c), through the lens of the AUC decomposition (presented in Section 2). These metrics are based on different components of the AUC and therefore capture different aspects of model discrimination. For consistency with the notation introduced above, we write AUC\mathrm{AUC} for the overall AUC, AUCg\mathrm{AUC}_{g} for the within-group AUC in subgroup gg, and xAUCi,j\mathrm{xAUC}_{i,j} for the cross-group AUC comparing individuals with the event from subgroup ii against individuals without the event from subgroup jj. We let p^yg\hat{p}_{y}^{g} denote the estimated probability assigned by a prediction model for binary outcome y∈{0,1}y\in\{0,1\} for an arbitrary individual in subgroup g∈{A,B}g\in\{A,B\}.

We only consider two subgroups (AA and BB) for simplicity. However, the metrics presented in this section can be extended to n>2n>2 subgroups by computing pairwise differences across all (n2)=n⁡(n−1)2\binom{n}{2}=\frac{n(n-1)}{2} distinct subgroup pairs.

A fairness metric MM may be operationalised using a pre-specified threshold θ\theta to determine whether a model satisfies the fairness notion at hand. For a metric MM where larger values indicate greater fairness, this may be defined as M≥θM\geq\theta. Conversely, for a metric where smaller values indicate greater fairness, this may be defined as M≤θM\leq\theta. The choice of θ\theta depends on the metric and application. For example, a parity-based metric, where smaller values indicate greater fairness, may use θ=0.05\theta=0.05 as the maximum acceptable difference.

3.1. Within-group AUC parity

Within-group AUC parity calculates the AUC within each subgroup and then estimates their absolute difference (Cheng et al., 2021):

(3) AUCparity=|AUCA−AUCB|.\displaystyle\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{parity}}=\left|\mathrm{AUC}_{A}-\mathrm{AUC}_{B}\right|.

A multiplicative variant has also been proposed (Byrd et al., 2023),

(4) AUCratio=AUCAAUCB.\displaystyle\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{ratio}}=\frac{\mathrm{AUC}_{A}}{\mathrm{AUC}_{B}}.

Both metrics quantify asymmetries in within-group discrimination only. For the difference-based metric (equation 3), the “optimal value” is 0, whereas for the ratio-based one (equation 4) a value of 1 indicates equal performance.

3.2. Cross-group AUC (xAUC) parity

Cross-group AUC (i.e., ranking of individuals with an event from one subgroup versus individuals without an event from the other subgroup) is calculated for each subgroup, the absolute difference is calculated across subgroups (Kallus and Zhou, 2019):

(5) xAUCparity=|xAUCA,B−xAUCB,A|.\displaystyle\mathrm{xAUC}_{\mathrm{parity}}=\left|\mathrm{xAUC}_{A,B}-\mathrm{xAUC}_{B,A}\right|.

A value of “0” means that the model is fair with respect to this metric (i.e., no cross-group discrimination asymmetry).

3.3. Gap to overall AUC

It has been proposed to compare within-group AUC with the overall AUC across subgroups (Albuquerque et al., 2024). This metric calculates the AUC in the overall sample, in the subgroup, and then takes the absolute difference:

(6) AUCgap=|AUC−AUCg|.\displaystyle\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{gap}}=\left|\mathrm{AUC}-\mathrm{AUC}_{g}\right|.

A value of “0” means that the model is fair with respect to this metric.

3.4. Equity-scaled AUC

Luo et al. (Luo et al., 2024) proposed penalising the overall AUC according to the within-group AUC parity:

(7) AUCES=AUC1+AUCparity.\displaystyle\mathrm{AUC_{ES}}=\frac{\mathrm{AUC}}{1+\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{parity}}}.

When AUCES=AUC\mathrm{AUC_{ES}}=\mathrm{AUC} (i.e., AUCparity=0\mathrm{AUC_{parity}}=0), the model is considered fair with respect to this metric.

3.5. Minimum-based metrics

Minimum-based metrics can evaluate discrimination according to the worst-performing subgroup (Diana et al., 2021; Mittelstadt et al., 2023), for example:

(8) AUCmin=min⁡{AUCA,AUCB}.\displaystyle\mathrm{AUC}_{\min}=\min\left\{\mathrm{AUC}_{A},\mathrm{AUC}_{B}\right\}.

Analogous definitions may be constructed using other AUC components. A model is considered fair when the minimum value of a metric of interest (e.g., A​U​CgAUC_{g}) is above a pre-specified threshold (e.g., min⁡{A​U​Cg}≥0.8\min\left\{AUC_{g}\right\}\geq 0.8).

3.6. 𝐱𝐀𝐔𝐂𝟏\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}

Also referred to as “Pairwise Ranking Fairness” (PRF), xAUC1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1} quantifies the probability that an individual with the event from subgroup gg is ranked above a randomly selected individual without the event from the population (Kallus and Zhou, 2019; Cui et al., 2023):

(9) xAUCA1\displaystyle\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{A} =P⁡(p^1A>p^0),\displaystyle=P(\hat{p}_{1}^{A}>\hat{p}_{0}),
(10) xAUCB1\displaystyle\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{B} =P⁡(p^1B>p^0).\displaystyle=P(\hat{p}_{1}^{B}>\hat{p}_{0}).

A higher xAUCg1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{g} indicates that individuals with the event from subgroup gg are more likely to be assigned higher estimated probabilities than individuals without the event in the overall population. A value of 0.50.5 corresponds to chance-level ranking, while values approaching 11 indicate better discrimination. Fairness is achieved when xAUCA1=xAUCB1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{A}=\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{B}, indicating that individuals with the event are ranked relative to the non-event population equally well across subgroups.

3.7. 𝐱𝐀𝐔𝐂𝟎\mathrm{xAUC}^{0}

Also referred to as “Subgroup AUC” (sAUC), xAUC0\mathrm{xAUC}^{0} quantifies the probability that a randomly selected individual without the event from subgroup gg is ranked below any individual with the event from the population (Kallus and Zhou, 2019; Meissen et al., 2024):

(11) xAUCA0\displaystyle\mathrm{xAUC}^{0}_{A} =P⁡(p^1>p^0A),\displaystyle=P(\hat{p}_{1}>\hat{p}_{0}^{A}),
(12) xAUCB0\displaystyle\mathrm{xAUC}^{0}_{B} =P⁡(p^1>p^0B).\displaystyle=P(\hat{p}_{1}>\hat{p}_{0}^{B}).

Similarly to xAUC1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1} (above), fairness is achieved when xAUCA0=xAUCB0\mathrm{xAUC}^{0}_{A}=\mathrm{xAUC}^{0}_{B}, indicating that individuals without the event are ranked relative to the event population equally well across subgroups.

3.8. 𝐱𝐀𝐔𝐂𝟏\mathrm{xAUC}^{1} and 𝐱𝐀𝐔𝐂𝟎\mathrm{xAUC}^{0} parity

These metrics estimate absolute differences in xAUC1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1} or xAUC0\mathrm{xAUC}^{0}, respectively, across subgroups (Meissen et al., 2024; Cui et al., 2023):

(13) xAUCparity1=|xAUCA1−xAUCB1|,\displaystyle\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{\mathrm{parity}}=\left|\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{A}-\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{B}\right|,
(14) xAUCparity0=|xAUCA0−xAUCB0|\displaystyle\mathrm{xAUC}^{0}_{\mathrm{parity}}=\left|\mathrm{xAUC}^{0}_{A}-\mathrm{xAUC}^{0}_{B}\right|

Fairness is achieved when xAUCparity1=0\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{\mathrm{parity}}=0 or xAUCparity0=0\mathrm{xAUC}^{0}_{\mathrm{parity}}=0.

4. Relationships between AUC-based fairness metrics

Several of the metrics presented above are either related to each other or to the overall AUC. For example, xAUC1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1} and xAUC0\mathrm{xAUC}^{0} can be expressed in terms of within-group and cross-group discrimination. For two subgroups AA and BB,

(15) xAUCA1\displaystyle\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{A} =p0Ap0​AUCA+p0Bp0​xAUCA,B,\displaystyle=\frac{p_{0}^{A}}{p_{0}}\,\mathrm{AUC}_{A}+\frac{p_{0}^{B}}{p_{0}}\,\mathrm{xAUC}_{A,B},
(16) xAUCB1\displaystyle\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{B} =p0Ap0​xAUCB,A+p0Bp0​AUCB,\displaystyle=\frac{p_{0}^{A}}{p_{0}}\,\mathrm{xAUC}_{B,A}+\frac{p_{0}^{B}}{p_{0}}\,\mathrm{AUC}_{B},
(17) xAUCA0\displaystyle\mathrm{xAUC}^{0}_{A} =p1Ap1​AUCA+p1Bp1​xAUCB,A,\displaystyle=\frac{p_{1}^{A}}{p_{1}}\,\mathrm{AUC}_{A}+\frac{p_{1}^{B}}{p_{1}}\,\mathrm{xAUC}_{B,A},
(18) xAUCB0\displaystyle\mathrm{xAUC}^{0}_{B} =p1Ap1​xAUCA,B+p1Bp1​AUCB.\displaystyle=\frac{p_{1}^{A}}{p_{1}}\,\mathrm{xAUC}_{A,B}+\frac{p_{1}^{B}}{p_{1}}\,\mathrm{AUC}_{B}.

These four quantities can in turn form a linear decomposition of the overall AUC,

(19) AUC=p1Ap1​xAUCA1+p1Bp1​xAUCB1=p0Ap0​xAUCA0+p0Bp0​xAUCB0,\displaystyle\mathrm{AUC}=\frac{p_{1}^{A}}{p_{1}}\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{A}+\frac{p_{1}^{B}}{p_{1}}\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{B}=\frac{p_{0}^{A}}{p_{0}}\mathrm{xAUC}^{0}_{A}+\frac{p_{0}^{B}}{p_{0}}\mathrm{xAUC}^{0}_{B},

providing an alternative representation of the overall model discrimination. Full proofs can be found in the Appendix.

Unlike the commonly reported within-group AUC, xAUC1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1} and xAUC0\mathrm{xAUC}^{0} incorporate both within- and cross-group discrimination. An alternative way to interpret these decompositions is through a part-whole perspective. xAUCA1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{A} and xAUCB1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{B} (and analogously xAUCA0\mathrm{xAUC}^{0}_{A} and xAUCB0\mathrm{xAUC}^{0}_{B}) form mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive contributions to the overall AUC, a property that conventional within-group AUCs lack since they omit the cross-group components.

Figure 1 summarises AUC components and AUC-based fairness metrics using AUC matrices. For a binary sensitive attribute, an AUC Matrix partitions all pairwise comparisons according to the subgroup membership of the individual with the event (rows) and the individual without the event (columns) (Chang et al., 2022). Each cell represents the probability that a randomly selected individual with an event from one subgroup has a higher estimated probability than a randomly selected individual without an event from the same or the other subgroup. The diagonal cells correspond to the within-group AUCs (AUCA\mathrm{AUC}_{A} and AUCB\mathrm{AUC}_{B}) and the off-diagonal cells to the cross-group AUCs (xAUCA,B\mathrm{xAUC}_{A,B} and xAUCB,A\mathrm{xAUC}_{B,A}).

5. Critical appraisal of AUC-based fairness metrics

In this section, we critically appraise each of the metrics in Section 3, in light of their formalisation and relationships with one another. Table 1 summarises the estimand targeted by each metric, our critical appraisal, and the corresponding recommendation. Recommendations are colour coded as recommended, use with caution, and generally not recommended. The table is intended as a practical guide for selecting AUC-based fairness metrics that align with an intended fairness objective whilst avoiding misleading interpretations. In general, we recommend reporting the overall AUC and the complete AUC matrix in Figure 1, which makes all within-group and cross-group AUC components explicit.

5.1. Within-group AUC parity

Within-group AUC parity (Cheng et al., 2021) compares the AUC calculated within each subgroup. It is appropriate when the fairness objective is to assess whether the model discriminates equally well within each subgroup. As demonstrated by the decomposition of the AUC, within-group AUCs ignore cross-group components, which may differ substantially even when subgroup specific AUCs are identical. Consequently, similar values of AUCA\mathrm{AUC}_{A} and AUCB\mathrm{AUC}_{B} may coexist with pronounced asymmetries in xAUCA,B\mathrm{xAUC}_{A,B} and xAUCB,A\mathrm{xAUC}_{B,A}, as well as with apparently paradoxical behaviour of the overall AUC due to non-collapsibility (Matos et al., 2026a). Conversely, substantial differences in within-group AUCs do not necessarily imply disparities in cross-group AUCs. This metric is recommended as the primary fairness metric for discrimination performance and should be reported alongside overall AUC. As the within-group AUC parity does not capture cross-group ranking disparities, the xAUC parity can provide important additional information, with cautious interpretation.

5.2. Cross-group AUC (xAUC) parity

Cross-group AUC (xAUC) parity is relevant when fairness concerns how individuals from different groups are ranked relative to one another (e.g., patients are ranked based on estimated probabilities or a binary decision is made after applying a single threshold). This metric provides information beyond the within-group AUC parity, which is important to comprehensively evaluate fairness in discrimination performance. However, as discussed by (Matos et al., 2026a), xAUC parity may be influenced by differences in outcome prevalence or calibration across subgroups. Consequently, improvements in xAUC parity may come at the expense of calibration disparity. Calibration has been recommended as a key domain of model performance (Van Calster et al., 2025) and fairness evaluation (Matos et al., 2026c; Matos et al., 2026b), unless only patient ranking matters (Kallus and Zhou, 2019). The xAUC parity should be used with caution and reported alongside within-group AUC parity and overall AUC. Interpreting this metric in isolation may be misleading because of its interplay with calibration and case-mix differences across subgroups.

5.3. Gap to overall AUC

The difference between the overall AUC and a subgroup specific AUC compares quantities that estimate fundamentally different aspects of discrimination. Subgroup specific AUC values quantify only within-group discrimination, whereas the overall AUC combines within-group and cross-group components. As these quantities are generally not directly comparable, this type of metric is generally not recommended for fairness checks.

5.4. Equity-Scaled AUC

Equity-Scaled AUC divides overall AUC by within-group AUC parity. The numerator (overall AUC) depends on both within- and cross-group AUCs, whereas the denominator depends only on within-group AUC parity. The metric implicitly assumes that fairness (“equity”) is captured by within-group parity alone, ignoring xAUCs. If used in isolation, this metric is difficult to interpret and susceptible to manipulation. This metric is generally not recommended.

5.5. Minimum-based fairness metrics

Minimum-based metrics focus exclusively on the worst-performing subgroup and aim to align with fairness definitions based on maximising the minimum subgroup performance (Mittelstadt et al., 2023). However, it is unclear how to interpret when reported in isolation, or how to act upon disparities flagged by this metric alone. This type of metric is generally not recommended.

5.6. 𝐱𝐀𝐔𝐂𝟏\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}

xAUCg1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{g} measures discrimination for individuals with the event (Y=1Y=1) in subgroup gg, by comparing their estimated probabilities against individuals without the event in the overall population. xAUCg1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{g} incorporates both within- and cross-group discrimination through a linear decomposition (Section 4). Consequently, it is less susceptible to Simpson-type paradoxes arising from ignoring cross-group AUCs. Whether this metric qualifies as a fairness metric on its own, or as an ancillary metric for fairness evaluation, is unclear. For example, for two subgroups, a comparison between xAUCA1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{A} and xAUCB1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{B} would be necessary to draw any fairness conclusion, and xAUCA1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{A} or xAUCB1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{B} do not say much about fairness on their own. This metric should be used with caution for each subgroup, when fairness is viewed from the perspective of individuals who do experience the event, and both within- and cross-group discrimination are relevant.

5.7. 𝐱𝐀𝐔𝐂𝟎\mathrm{xAUC}^{0}

xAUC0\mathrm{xAUC}^{0} measures discrimination for individuals without the event (Y=0Y=0) in subgroup gg. Like xAUC1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}, it combines within- and cross-group discrimination into a linear decomposition of the overall AUC. This metric should be used with caution when fairness is viewed from the perspective of individuals who do not experience the event, and both within- and cross-group discrimination are relevant.

5.8. 𝐱𝐀𝐔𝐂𝟏\mathrm{xAUC}^{1} and 𝐱𝐀𝐔𝐂𝟎\mathrm{xAUC}^{0} Parity

These metrics should be used with caution whenever the use of xAUC1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1} or xAUC0\mathrm{xAUC}^{0} is deemed justifiable and relevant. Fairness conclusions based on the xAUCparity1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{\mathrm{parity}} may be particularly relevant in positively polar decisions (i.e., patients benefit from selection, e.g., being selected for an organ transplant). An eligible patient from subgroup gg should always be ranked (by the model) above an ineligible patient from any subgroup (Paulus and Kent, 2020), regardless of subgroup membership. Contrary to xAUCparity1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{\mathrm{parity}}, xAUCparity0\mathrm{xAUC}^{0}_{\mathrm{parity}} is particularly relevant in negatively polar decisions (i.e, patients benefit from exclusion, e.g., quarantining patients at high infectious risk). An ineligible patient from subgroup gg should always be ranked (by the model) below an eligible patient from any subgroup (Paulus and Kent, 2020), regardless of subgroup membership.

6. Clinical example

The European System for Cardiac Operative Risk Evaluation (EuroSCORE) II (Nashef et al., 2012) is a clinical prediction model developed using data from 22,381 patients across 154 hospitals in 43 countries. It uses demographic and clinical predictors to estimate the probability of in-hospital mortality following cardiac surgery and achieved an AUC of 0.81. Although the model has been widely validated (Kalender et al., 2014; Garcia-Valentin et al., 2016; Chalmers et al., 2013), its fairness has been rarely assessed (Silverborn et al., 2023). As a publicly-available model, EuroSCORE II may be used for, among others, three potential use cases, which we summarise below:

  1. (1)

    Risk estimation (continuous scale): The model output can be used to communicate risk to patients and caregivers, benchmark institutional outcomes, or stratify populations’ risk.

  2. (2)

    Binary decision: A threshold (set by clinicians, hospitals, or health authorities) is applied, to facilitate surgical decision-making or serve as a quality control benchmark to stratify outcomes between low- and high-risk interventions. Decision thresholds are often arbitrarily set by optimising a statistical criterion.

  3. (3)

    Patient ranking: In certain contexts, only the ordering of patients matters and the absolute magnitude of estimated risk is irrelevant. For example, a prioritisation system for surgical waiting lists might rank patients according to their estimated risk and relative ordering.

In this section, we consider these three use cases as context for the interpretation of AUC-based fairness metrics, in three simulated performance scenarios. The Python code used to generate the simulated data, AUC-based fairness metrics, and figures presented in this section is publicly available as an executable Jupyter notebook on Google Colab.

6.1. Simulations and discrimination performance scenarios

We simulate three scenarios with varying discrimination performance across subgroups, defined by patient sex at birth (binary sensitive attribute). Simulations were conducted by generating estimated probabilities distributions separately for patients with and without events within each sex subgroup. For each scenario, we fixed the proportion of male and female patients (pM=0.8p^{M}=0.8, pF=0.2p^{F}=0.2) and the outcome prevalences (πM=0.02\pi^{M}=0.02, πF=0.03\pi^{F}=0.03), following the patient characteristics reported in (Silverborn et al., 2023). Estimated probability distributions were simulated using truncated normal distributions with support on the interval [0,1][0,1]. Discrimination was controlled by specifying the means of the distributions patients not experiencing an event (μ0F\mu_{0}^{F} and μ0M\mu_{0}^{M}) and experiencing an event (μ1F\mu_{1}^{F} and μ1M\mu_{1}^{M}). Simulation parameters are summarised in Table 2. The resulting AUC metrics are reported in Table 3. Each scenario is examined below.

Scenario (i): Substantial within-group AUC disparity

Suppose the model’s overall AUC is 0.85, with within-group AUCs of 0.88 for male patients and 0.73 for female patients. However, there is a difference in cross-group AUC in the opposite direction, with xAUCM,F=0.67\mathrm{xAUC}_{M,F}=0.67 and xAUCF,M=0.92\mathrm{xAUC}_{F,M}=0.92. Metrics are summarised in Figure 2(a).

Scenario (ii): Improving worst-performing subgroup performance

The model is updated to improve discrimination in female patients, resulting in AUCfemale\mathrm{AUC_{female}} increasing from 0.73 to 0.80, whilst performance in male patients remains unchanged (AUCmale\mathrm{AUC_{male}} = 0.88). Despite this improvement, the overall AUC decreases from 0.85 to 0.84, which is explained by a more pronounced disparity in cross-group AUC components: xAUCM,F=0.44\mathrm{xAUC}_{M,F}=0.44 and xAUCF,M=0.99\mathrm{xAUC}_{F,M}=0.99 (see Figure 2(b)).

Scenario (iii): Degrading best-performing subgroup performance

Suppose AUC parity is now achieved, such that the model appears fair from the standpoint of within-group AUC parity (AUCM=AUCF=0.86\mathrm{AUC_{M}}=\mathrm{AUC_{F}}=0.86). Improving AUCF\mathrm{AUC_{F}} came at the cost of degrading AUCM\mathrm{AUC_{M}}. Despite within-group AUC parity, there still is a disparity in cross-group AUC: xAUCM,F=0.53\mathrm{xAUC}_{M,F}=0.53 and xAUCF,M=0.98\mathrm{xAUC}_{F,M}=0.98, which results in an overall AUC of 0.84 (see Figure 2(c)).

6.2. Fairness interpretation across use cases and scenarios

6.2.1. Model use case (1): Risk estimation

Let us assume that the developed model is used to communicate risk. The model estimated probabilities are directly used, and no decision thresholds are applied. We consider three scenarios.

Scenario (i): Substantial AUC disparity

A difference in within-group AUCs exists (AUCparity=|0.88−0.73|=0.15\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{parity}}=\left|0.88-0.73\right|=0.15). However, when examining xAUC\mathrm{xAUC} components, the picture differs: xAUCM,F=0.67\mathrm{xAUC}_{M,F}=0.67 and xAUCF,M=0.92\mathrm{xAUC}_{F,M}=0.92, which means that female patients with an event would be better separated from male patients without an event (xAUCF,M\mathrm{xAUC}_{F,M}), than the other other way around (xAUCM,F\mathrm{xAUC}_{M,F}), resulting in a cross-group disparity of 0.25 (xAUCparity=|0.67−0.92|=0.25\mathrm{xAUC}_{\mathrm{parity}}=\left|0.67-0.92\right|=0.25). Here, AUCparity\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{parity}} does not provide a complete picture of unfairness, and xAUCparity\mathrm{xAUC}_{\mathrm{parity}} is informative.

When examining xAUC1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1} metrics, the interplay between within- and cross-group discrimination is summarised: xAUCM1=0.84\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{M}=0.84 and xAUCF1=0.88\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{F}=0.88, resulting in a less pronounced disparity according to these metrics: xAUCparity1=|0.84−0.88|=0.04\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{\mathrm{parity}}=\left|0.84-0.88\right|=0.04. This results from the fact that male patients are better off according to within-group AUCs, whereas female patients are better off in terms of cross-group AUC. Here, xAUCparity1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{\mathrm{parity}} is not exactly zero, meaning that the model is not considered “perfectly fair” according to this metric, which happens because the “advantage” that female patients have in cross-group discrimination outweighs the “advantage” that male patients have in within-group discrimination.

Key takeaways: Within-group AUC disparity can co-exist with cross-group AUC disparity, underscoring the importance of reporting both within-group AUC parity and cross-group AUC parity metrics.

Scenario (ii): Improving worst-performing subgroup performance

In this new scenario, the difference in within-group AUC has decreased, thanks to increase in AUCF\mathrm{AUC}_{F} from 0.73 to 0.80, while AUCM\mathrm{AUC}_{M} was kept at 0.88. As depicted on the right-hand side of Figure 2(b), this is explained by the fact that the distribution of model estimated probabilities for male patients did not change, only female patients’ distribution did. Nonetheless, this resulted in changes in cross-group AUC values that affected both subgroups’ performance. xAUCM,F\mathrm{xAUC}_{M,F} further deteriorated, decreasing from 0.67, in Scenario (i), to 0.44 here, whereas xAUCF,M\mathrm{xAUC}_{F,M} improved, going from 0.92, in Scenario (i), to 0.99 here. As a result, overall AUC degraded slightly, going from 0.85 in Scenario (i), to 0.84, meaning that the model discrimination improvement in terms of AUCF\mathrm{AUC}_{F} did not compensate for losses in cross-group discrimination (in which both xAUCM,F\mathrm{xAUC}_{M,F} and xAUCF,M\mathrm{xAUC}_{F,M} changed).

As a result of these model changes, xAUCM1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{M} declines from 0.84 in Scenario (i) to 0.79 here, highlighting the contribution of both AUCM\mathrm{AUC}_{M} and xAUCM,F\mathrm{xAUC}_{M,F} to xAUCM1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{M}. The verified decline in xAUCM1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{M} also shows that, even though the model estimated probabilities for male patients did not change, discrimination declined for these patients, overall, due to the contribution of cross-group ranking. On the other hand, xAUCF1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{F} improved, going from 0.88, in Scenario (i), to 0.95 in this Scenario (ii), which stems from the improved xAUCF,M\mathrm{xAUC}_{F,M} and AUCF\mathrm{AUC}_{F}.

In terms of fairness metrics, the improved AUCF\mathrm{AUC}_{F} results in a lower AUCparity=|0.88−0.80|=0.08\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{parity}}=\left|0.88-0.80\right|=0.08, meaning that the model in Scenario (ii) is fairer than the model in Scenario (i) in terms of within-group discrimination. However, xAUCp​a​r​i​t​y=|0.44−0.99|=0.55\mathrm{xAUC}_{parity}=\left|0.44-0.99\right|=0.55, which is substantially higher than the 0.25 disparity in cross-group discrimination from Scenario (i), meaning that this new model is more unequal in terms of cross-group discrimination, to a greater extent than the fairness improvement in within-group discrimination. The xAUC1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1} metrics show this: xAUCparity1=|0.79−0.95|=0.16\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{\mathrm{parity}}=\left|0.79-0.95\right|=0.16, an increase in disparity when compared to Scenario (i) (0.04). This parity metric indicates greater inequality across male and female patients, when taking into consideration both within- and cross-group discrimination.

An important artefact in this Scenario (ii) is the apparent improvement in “subgroup AUCs” (i.e., improvement of female patients’ within-group AUC), but a decline in overall AUC. This almost paradoxical finding is a consequence of the AUC non-collapsibility (Matos et al., 2026a), and highlights the importance of considering and reporting cross-group AUCs. The phenomena we describe here complicate interpretation and communication with stakeholders. What was intended to be a “level-up” strategy, improving performance (measured in terms of within-group AUC) of the worse-off subgroup (female patients), without compromising the better-off subgroup (male patients), inadvertently produced a “level-down” effect for male patients through changes in cross-group discrimination.

Key takeaways: Improving the performance of a worse-performing subgroup in terms of within-group AUC, without any model change to the model estimated probabilities of the better-performing subgroup, may nonetheless result in a deterioration of the unchanged subgroup’s cross-group AUC. If such deterioration is in greater magnitude than the within-group improvement, a (seemingly paradoxical) degradation of overall AUC can occur.

Scenario (iii): Degrading best-performing subgroup performance

In this final scenario, within-group AUC parity is achieved (AUCparity=|0.86−0.86|=0\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{parity}}=\left|0.86-0.86\right|=0) thanks to a model modification that shifts the estimated probabilities distributions of both male and female patients (in Scenario (ii) only female patients’ distribution had been affected). As a result, AUCM\mathrm{AUC}_{M} declines to 0.86, from 0.88 in Scenario (i) and (ii), equalising AUCF\mathrm{AUC}_{F} at 0.86, which raises from 0.80 in Scenario (ii). This model modification also results in an increase of xAUCM,F\mathrm{xAUC}_{M,F} from 0.44 in Scenario (ii) to 0.53 here, and a slight decrease in xAUCF,M\mathrm{xAUC}_{F,M} from 0.99 in Scenario (ii) to 0.98 here, making xAUCparity=|0.53−0.98|=0.45\mathrm{xAUC}_{\mathrm{parity}}=\left|0.53-0.98\right|=0.45. Overall AUC is kept at 0.84, which is below both AUCM=AUCF=0.86\mathrm{AUC}_{M}=\mathrm{AUC}_{F}=0.86, an “artefact” of AUC’s non-collapsibility (Matos et al., 2026a) that is possible here due to cross-group AUC values (xAUCM,F=0.53\mathrm{xAUC}_{M,F}=0.53 and xAUCF,M=0.98\mathrm{xAUC}_{F,M}=0.98), which together outweigh the within-group values (AUCM=AUCF=0.86\mathrm{AUC}_{M}=\mathrm{AUC}_{F}=0.86).

Additionally, xAUCM1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{M} increased from 0.79 in Scenario (ii) to 0.80 here, and xAUCF1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{F} from 0.95 in Scenario (ii) to 0.96 here, resulting in xAUCparity1=0.16\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{\mathrm{parity}}=0.16, the same exact value achieved in Scenario (ii). The fact that xAUCparity1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1}_{\mathrm{parity}} did not change from Scenario (ii) to (iii) underscores the importance of considering both within- and cross-group metrics to understand sources of potential unfairness. Despite the apparent deterioration captured by AUCM\mathrm{AUC}_{M} (AUCM=0.88\mathrm{AUC}_{M}=0.88 in Scenario (ii), to AUCM=0.86\mathrm{AUC}_{M}=0.86 here), male patients achieve better performance in terms of model discrimination, overall, because of the cross-group AUC contributions (xAUCM,F=0.44\mathrm{xAUC}_{M,F}=0.44 in Scenario (ii), raised to xAUCM,F=0.53\mathrm{xAUC}_{M,F}=0.53 here).

Key takeaways: Within-group AUC parity can co-exist with cross-group AUC disparity. If cross-group AUC disparity is sufficiently large, the resulting overall AUC could be lower (or higher) than both subgroups’ within-group AUC values. This artefact is created by AUC non-collapsibility and may complicate communication with stakeholders.

6.2.2. Model use case (2): Binary decision

Let us assume now that this last model – Scenario (iii) – is used for binary decisions, i.e., a threshold is applied to model estimated probabilities. Two plausible strategies could follow.

Strategy (i): One single threshold is applied to all patients.

When a model is used to support decision-making, all patients (regardless of their subgroups) use a common decision threshold. With such strategy, relying on within-group discrimination metrics (AUCg\mathrm{AUC_{g}}) alone is insufficient. Cross-group AUC terms are as important as within-group AUC values because together they determine how estimated probabilities are ordered when a single threshold is applied.

In this Scenario (iii) model, as shown in Figure 2(c), even when within-group AUCs are identical (AUCM=AUCF=0.86\mathrm{AUC}_{M}=\mathrm{AUC}_{F}=0.86), xAUCM,F=0.53\mathrm{xAUC}_{M,F}=0.53 versus xAUCF,M=0.98\mathrm{xAUC}_{F,M}=0.98 indicate that it is only slightly above that chance (53% probability) that male patients with an event are assigned estimated probabilities that are higher than the ones assigned to female patients without an event, whereas female patients with an event will have a higher estimated probability than male patients without an event most times (98% probability). In settings where the decision is polar (i.e., patients benefit from selection (Paulus and Kent, 2020)), this asymmetry disadvantages male patients, as female patients are far more likely to exceed the decision threshold. With a single decision threshold, this asymmetry would result in unequal downstream decisions (which could be captured by threshold-dependent fairness metrics (Matos et al., 2026c)).

Two main mechanisms can explain how within-group AUC parity can coexist with cross-group AUC disparities. First, differences in outcome prevalence across subgroups may reflect differences in underlying risk, leading to shifts in the distributions of estimated probabilities. For example, female patients have a higher outcome prevalence (πF=0.03\pi^{F}=0.03) than male patients (πM=0.02\pi^{M}=0.02), which may result in systematically higher estimated probabilities. Such differences can be monitored using “mean score parity” metrics (Matos et al., 2026a; Matos et al., 2026c). Second, differences in calibration across subgroups can lead to asymmetric cross-group rankings, even when within-group AUCs are identical. For instance, if risk is systematically underestimated for male patients but not for female patients, the resulting differences in estimated probabilities may introduce cross-group AUC disparities (Matos et al., 2026a).

Key takeaways: Applying a single decision threshold to a model with AUCparity=0\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{parity}}=0 but xAUCparity≫0\mathrm{xAUC}_{\mathrm{parity}}\gg 0 is expected to result in unequal downstream decisions, underscoring the importance of reporting within- and cross-group discrimination to prevent downstream unequal decisions.

Strategy (ii): Subgroup specific thresholds are defined and applied.

When cross-group AUC disparities exist (xAUCparity=0.45\mathrm{xAUC}_{\mathrm{parity}}=0.45) but no within-group AUC disparities exist (AUCparity=0\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{parity}}=0), as seen in Scenario (iii), subgroup specific thresholds should be considered. If distinct decision thresholds are specified for each subgroup, cross-group comparisons no longer directly influence decision-making and the within-group AUC parity becomes the only consequential fairness metric in this context. Fairness considerations in terms of discrimination only concern within-group AUCs, as cross-group “competition” is eliminated and cross-group ranking ceases to be a consideration. Subgroup specific thresholds (such as “race corrections” (Vyas et al., 2020)) are not uncommon in medicine.

Key takeaways: Subgroup specific decision thresholds should be considered when xAUCparity≫0\mathrm{xAUC}_{\mathrm{parity}}\gg 0. With subgroup specific decision thresholds, cross-group ranking ceases to be a consideration, and fairness in terms of discrimination solely depends on AUCparity\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{parity}}.

6.2.3. Model use case (3): Patient ranking

Finally, let us assume that the model is being used to rank patients. In settings where only the ordering of individuals matters, such as surgery prioritisation, absolute risk magnitudes become irrelevant. Decisions in this context are inherently polar, as patients are “competing” against each other (and against the “system”) to get an estimated probability that places them on top of the list (Paulus and Kent, 2020). Traditional within-group AUC parity-based fairness analyses are insufficient to assess ranking/discrimination fairness, and xAUC components are equally relevant. Metrics that combine both within- and cross-group AUCs, such as the xAUC1\mathrm{xAUC}^{1} and xAUC0\mathrm{xAUC}^{0}, are therefore well suited to summarise fairness in terms of discrimination in this setting (Figure 2).

7. Conclusions and Recommendations

In this paper, we examined eight AUC-based fairness metrics, characterised their estimands, critically appraised their interpretation using a clinical example, and provided guidance on how to use and interpret these metrics in the context of different types of fairness assessments. The use and interpretation of these metrics are inherently context-dependent, and no single metric can fully capture the complexity of fairness in model discrimination when subgroups coexist. Therefore, we recommend reporting the AUC matrix as a whole, containing the overall AUC and all within- and cross-group AUC components, to allow discrimination performance to be evaluated comprehensively. When fairness metrics are needed (for example, when more than two subgroups coexist, resulting in large AUC matrices, or when a summary measure of fairness is preferable), we recommend within-group AUC parity as the primary fairness metric for discrimination performance. Cross-group AUC parity can provide important additional information on cross-group ranking disparities but should be used with caution due to its potential conflict with calibration and case-mix differences across subgroups. Transparent reporting of population characteristics (Matos et al., 2026a) and adherence to TRIPOD+AI (Collins et al., 2024b) are essential for meaningful fairness evaluations of clinical predictive AI. Although this paper focused on discrimination and AUC-based fairness metrics, their interplay with calibration is important and warrants further investigation, especially regarding the potential trade-offs between discrimination and calibration fairness.

Ethical Considerations Statement

This study aims to improve evaluation of fairness in clinical prediction models. We highlight the limitations of existing AUC-based fairness metrics and provide recommendations for their appropriate use and interpretation. Misinterpretation or inappropriate application of these metrics could lead to misleading conclusions about model performance and fairness, potentially affecting healthcare decisions and exacerbating existing health inequalities. Our recommendations aim to support more transparent and comprehensive fairness assessments, while recognising that statistical fairness metrics alone cannot establish whether a clinical prediction model is fair or safe for deployment.
